extracted.intended_audience: patent examiners, applicants, and patent attorneys operating in AMS (Asian Member States)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examination and drafting of patent applications in AMS covering subject-matter exclusions (computer programs, medical methods, plants/animals, microorganisms), unity of invention, and clarity/claim-drafting requirements. Aimed at determining patentable subject-matter, assessing unity, and ensuring claims satisfy clarity/support requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical effect requirement for computer programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Since patentability of computer programs depends on a technical effect, the claims must be so drafted as to include all the technical features of the invention which are essential for the technical effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where patentability is admitted then, generally speaking, product, process and use claims would be allowable. Ensure claims include the technical features that produce the technical effect; mere program code 'as such' without technical character is not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Four-step approach to computer program 'as such' exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: One approach consists in applying the following four steps: (1) Properly construe the claim; (2) Identify the actual contribution made by the invention; (3) Determine whether the actual contribution falls solely within the excluded subject matter or not 'as such'; (4) Determine whether the actual or alleged contribution is actually technical in nature ('Technical contribution').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must construe the invention from the claims and specification, objectively assess the contribution (not be bound by applicant's statement), and only proceed to other substantive aspects (novelty, inventive step) if the invention passes the technical character test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of 'computer-implemented invention'
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Computer-implemented invention' is a term intended to cover claims involving computers, computer networks or other programmable apparatus wherein at least one feature is implemented by means of a computer program.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between a computer program (sequence of executable instructions) and a computer-implemented method (method performed on a computer).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of computer-implemented methods and technical means
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims directed to a computer-implemented method cannot be objected to on the ground that they are not patentable subject matter because any method involving the use of technical means (e.g. a computer) and any technical means itself (e.g. a computer or a computer-readable storage medium) have technical character and thus represent inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims to emphasise technical means/features; include technical implementation details where relevant to establish technical character.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exclusion: methods for treatment of the human or animal body (surgery, therapy, diagnosis)
rubrics_metrics.description: AMS’ patent laws exclude methods for treatment of the human or animal body for diagnosis, surgery and therapy from patentability. The purpose is to ensure practitioners are not hindered by patents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether claimed method is a treatment/diagnosis performed on the living body. If so, method claims will be excluded even if only one step defines a therapeutic activity. Consider exceptions for products/instruments for use in such methods (these are patentable).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of therapy criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: As long as the treatment cures, prevents or alleviates a disease, the treatment would constitute a method of therapy whether performed by the patient, practitioner, or automated system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Non-therapeutic treatments (e.g., purely cosmetic treatments, contraception) may be patentable. A therapeutic step in a claim (e.g., administering a substance prophylactically) can render the method claim unpatentable. Therapeutic instruments and products for use in therapy are not excluded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic instruments and products exception
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutic instruments or apparatus for use in methods of surgery/therapy/diagnosis are not excluded from patentability. Likewise, products, in particular substances or compositions, for use in therapeutic methods are patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims directed to apparatus, compositions, or products for use in treatment are acceptable even if the method of use is unpatentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of diagnosis exclusion and required phases
rubrics_metrics.description: A method of diagnosis must include the deductive step which leads to a diagnosis and a recommended treatment. Methods of diagnosis are excluded only if performed on the body. The claim must include method steps relating to all of the following phases: (i) the examination phase (collection of data), (ii) the comparison of these data with standard values, (iii) the finding of any significant deviation (a symptom), (iv) the attribution of the deviation to a particular clinical picture (deductive decision/diagnosis).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extra-corporeal diagnostic methods (e.g., tests on blood samples not returned to body) may be patentable. Diagnostic methods applied to dead bodies or to tissues/fluids not returned to the same body are not excluded. Ensure claims either omit the deductive/treatment recommendation step or are drafted to avoid being limited to on-body application if patentability is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plants, animals and 'essentially biological' processes exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: AMS patent laws exclude plant and animal varieties from patentability. The question whether a process is 'essentially biological' depends on the degree of technical intervention by man; significant technical intervention can make the process patentable. Transgenic plants and genetically modified animals (except Thailand) and methods of making them would be patentable. Product claims for plant or animal varieties cannot be allowed even if produced by microbiological processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claimed process includes sufficient technical steps/intervention (e.g., genetic manipulation, cloning) to be considered non-essentially biological. Examples: simple selective breeding is essentially biological (excluded); treating plant with growth stimulant is technical (not excluded).

rubrics_metrics.name: Naturally occurring micro-organism and 'microbiological process' treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Micro-organism' includes algae, bacteria, fungi, protozoa and viruses. Some AMS consider naturally occurring microorganisms discoveries (not patentable), but most AMS allow microorganisms to be patentable. PCT guidance: exclusion for plants/animals/processes does not apply to microbiological processes or their products; 'microbiological process' covers processes involving microbiological material including genetic engineering; 'product of a microbiological process' covers plasmids and viruses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to microbiological processes and products are generally allowable; however, plant material able to regenerate a full plant may be excluded if the plant originated from an essentially biological process. Draft claims to emphasise technical/man-made modifications to microorganisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pharmaceutical products, drugs and foodstuffs generally patentable (except LDCs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pharmaceutical product, drug and foodstuff are not excluded from patentability in AMS except in Least Developed Countries (LDCs), per WTO/TRIPS transitional arrangements until at least January 2033.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware of national variations in LDCs where pharmaceutical patents may not be protected; otherwise draft conventional pharma claims as patentable subject-matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of invention requirement (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application can claim only one invention or a group of closely related inventions. Unity of invention requires that the claims relate to a single invention, or at most a group of inventions linked by a single general inventive concept; inventions share a 'single general inventive concept' if the claims as interpreted in light of the description/drawings have the same or corresponding special technical features that achieve the same technical effect or solve the same technical problem over the prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is relevant in pre-grant proceedings only; lack of unity is not a ground for revocation after grant. A finding of lack of clarity is not by itself sufficient to find lack of unity. Divisional applications are generally allowed irrespective of unity objections (except Thailand).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of unity of invention / determining 'special technical features'
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner assesses unity by determining whether two or more inventions detailed in the claims have the same or corresponding special technical features. An examiner determines 'special technical features' from the claims in light of the description, drawings and common general knowledge as of the filing date. 'Same' and 'corresponding' means the features achieve the same technical effect or solve the same technical problem (e.g., alternative solutions or interrelated features).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a metal spring and a block of rubber may correspond because both achieve resilience. If special technical feature of one invention is the same as or corresponds to that of another, unity is fulfilled. If not, only the inventions belonging to the unified group are designated for examination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimum reasoning methodology for lack of unity findings
rubrics_metrics.description: To assess non-unitary subject-matter, the patent office may apply 'minimum reasoning' methodology: identify common or corresponding subject-matter, explain why this subject-matter cannot provide a single general inventive concept due to lack of same/corresponding special technical features, and explain why there is no technical relationship among the groups of inventions if not apparent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The analysis may include identification of non-common technical features and why claims may be grouped together, statement of why these features/demonstrated technical properties are different, and explanation of why their technical properties are different. Provide sufficient (minimum) reasoning rather than narrow literal approaches. Examples and PCT paragraphs cited for illustration.

rubrics_metrics.name: A priori vs a posteriori assessment of unity
rubrics_metrics.description: Lack of unity may be assessed 'a priori' (before considering prior art) or 'a posteriori' (after taking prior art into account). Most AMS use both approaches; Lao PDR uses only a priori. The examiner usually forms a prima facie unity opinion before the search and reconsiders in light of documents found; substantive examination further reconsiders unity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A feature considered common a priori may be shown to be not contributory over prior art after search, leading to lack of unity a posteriori. Benefit of doubt afforded to applicant; no rigid rules between extremes—assess on merits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of unity with regard to prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: An examiner determines 'special technical features' based on claims, description and common general knowledge. Lack of unity may become apparent after a document found in search shows that a linking feature lacks novelty or is obvious, so claims joined thereby no longer share a common inventive concept. If groups of inventions have the same corresponding special technical feature, unity is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example provided: Claim 1 polymeric compound A and Claim 2 packaging composed of A both share polymeric compound A as special technical feature that contributes over prior art — unity present. If an independent claim does not avoid prior art, carefully consider whether dependent claims still have inventive link.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal and remedies for a unity objection
rubrics_metrics.description: If examiner finds lack of unity, the examiner will inform the applicant, indicate inventions not deemed subject of examination, and describe reasons. The applicant should be given five options: appeal/counter statement, amend claims, delete claims, file divisional application(s), or abandon/withdraw the application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In some jurisdictions (e.g., Cambodia, Viet Nam) unity rejections raised in office action may not be appealable but can be countered in writing; in all AMS any person aggrieved may appeal to court (except Thailand where Director-General decision is final).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity requirement for the invention (claims, description, abstract, drawings)
rubrics_metrics.description: All AMS require the abstract, claims, description, and drawings, if any, to be clear and concise. If the description, claims or drawings are so unclear that no meaningful opinion can be formed on novelty, inventive step or industrial applicability, examination may be restricted to claims or parts that are sufficiently clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Issues of clarity should be raised separately from novelty/inventive step. If examiner cannot establish an opinion on a claim, they may object for lack of clarity. Clarity of claims is vital to assessing novelty, inventive step and industrial applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: PCT claim requirements: define protection, be clear/concise, supported by description
rubrics_metrics.description: The PCT Guidelines require that claims must (i) define the matter for which protection is sought; (ii) be clear and concise; and (iii) be fully supported by the description. Claims must be drafted in terms of the 'technical features of the invention'. The two-part form should be used 'whenever appropriate'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these requirements to individual claims and claims as a whole. Use two-part form where helpful; ensure support in description for claimed features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims should not rely on references to description/drawings except when absolutely necessary
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims must not, in respect of the technical features of the invention, rely on references to the description or drawings 'except where absolutely necessary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cross-references from claims to descriptive portions or figures; if unavoidable, justify necessity. Reliance on references can be grounds for clarity objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible content in claims: formulae and tables
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims, as well as the description, 'may contain chemical or mathematical formulae' but not drawings. 'Any claim may contain tables' but 'only if the subject matter of the claim makes the use of tables desirable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use formulae and tables where they materially assist in defining the claimed subject-matter; do not include drawings in claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of claims and product vs activity distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Two basic kinds of claim: claims to a physical entity (product, apparatus) and claims to an activity (process, use). Product-by-process, means-plus-function, and product/apparatus limitations in process claims are recognised and subject to specific PCT guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose appropriate claim category; be mindful of special rules (e.g., product-by-process treatment, means-plus-function interpretation). See PCT ISPE GL cross-references for details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent and dependent claims requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: All applications will contain one or more independent main claims directed to the essential features of the invention. Dependent claims concerning specific forms must include all the features of at least one independent claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure dependent claims fall within scope of an independent claim and include the essential features of the invention. Dependent claims cannot omit essential features required to define the invention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of claims by a Person Skilled in the Art (PSIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims should be interpreted the same way for search and examination. Each claim should be read giving the words the ordinary meaning/scope that would be attributed by a PSIA at the relevant time, unless the description gives words a special meaning by explicit definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft claims with PSIA ordinary meaning in mind; where special definitions are needed, define terms clearly in the description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and closed claims / transition phrases affect search and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: In evaluating novelty or inventive step, the examiner should consider the transition phrase used (e.g., 'consisting of', 'comprising', 'characterized by', 'consisting essentially of'), as the subject matter to be searched depends on the transition phrase.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select transition phrases deliberately to achieve intended claim scope. Understand how search/examination will treat 'open' vs 'closed' language.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions for clarity of claim language (PSIA boundary certainty)
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of the terms of a claim must be clear for a Person Skilled in the Art from the wording of the claim alone. If a PSIA can determine the boundaries of the claimed invention with a reasonable degree of certainty, the claim complies with clarity. Breadth is not necessarily lack of clarity. An independent claim should clearly specify all essential features needed to define the invention (except those implied by generic terms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess clarity in light of application disclosure, prior art, and PSIA interpretation at time of invention. For process claims, ensure process as claimed necessarily results in the claimed product when carried out reasonably; otherwise internal inconsistency leads to lack of clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of terms and expressions that may cause lack of clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: In the AMS, the following terms when used in claims and descriptions may be regarded as ambiguous, inadequate, unclear or too broad and thus lead to lack of clarity: indefinite/relative words (e.g., 'thin', 'wide', 'strong'); terms of approximation (e.g., 'about', 'approximately', 'somewhat'); ambiguous adverbs (e.g., 'preferably', 'more preferably', 'in particular', 'substantially', 'mostly', 'similarly', 'for example', 'such as'); references (e.g., 'as described in part...', 'as illustrated in figure...'); trademarks/trade names/proper names; and multiple outcomes e.g., 'and/or'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid or carefully justify use of such terms. Where approximate terms are necessary, provide measurable ranges or definitions in the description. Avoid vague references and ensure terms are defined or used where their meaning is clear to PSIA.
